body: gate-a-verify-block, which nobody called and which could not have worked.

author: reek
body: It hashed with sha256 -- eight 32-bit WORDS -- and compared the result against a byte digest over 32 elements, so it read a word against a byte eight times and then walked twenty-four elements off the end of an eight-element list. Both are List Integer, so nothing in the type system objected, and no test existed to notice. That is the whole reason it survived: a function nobody calls and nobody tests is not code, it is a rumour.

author: reek
body: The first check is the one that would have caught it: a block hashed and compared against its OWN correct byte digest must pass. Under the old code that comparison was word-against-byte and could not pass.

author: reek
body: The rest are the refusals. A digest of the wrong length is a mismatch rather than a walk off the end, and a flipped byte anywhere -- first, middle, last -- is a mismatch. The last-byte case matters most: a comparison that stops early passes everything up to where it stopped.

author: reek
body: A real digest is thirty-two bytes, not eight words.

author: reek
body: A short digest is a mismatch, not a read past the end. This is the shape the old code walked into on every call.

author: reek
body: A different block does not match the first block's digest.
